design_detail: Systematic review with multivariable mixed-effects (multilevel) meta-regression of randomized controlled trials of racemic ketamine or esketamine against a control condition for depression (eClinicalMedicine 2023;62:102127; received 8 February 2023, revised 9 July, accepted 17 July, published 3 August 2023). PROSPERO CRD42021221157. Five databases searched to 13 April 2023 in any language, plus reference lists and trial registries. 49 trials (45 published, 3 known only from registry results, and the authors' own KADS trial, then under review), 3299 participants, 72 ketamine arms and 52 control arms. Model: R metafor, restricted maximum likelihood, study as random effect, linear and quadratic time, formulation (racemic or esketamine), a two-level dose category and their interaction as fixed effects; every reported time point within a window entered the model. Outcomes: standardised mean difference (SMD) in depression severity and odds ratios (OR) for response, remission and all-cause dropout, in three windows: acute (4 hours to 3 days after the first dose), during repeated dosing (day 4 to the last dose) and after the last dose of a course (up to 28 days). The dose category is the review's classification of trial conditions: 'High' for an intravenous racemic-equivalent dose of 0.5 mg/kg or more (or titration up to it) or intranasal dosing predominantly at 84 mg or more, 'Low' otherwise. Crossover trials contributed first-period data. No funding.
can_establish: The average difference between ketamine (racemic or esketamine, as given in randomized trials up to April 2023) and control conditions in depression scores, response, remission and all-cause dropout, by time window after the first dose, during repeated dosing and up to four weeks after the last dose, and how those averages differ across the review's formulation and dose categories within one model.
cannot_establish: Whether racemic ketamine is more effective than esketamine, or a 'High' dose more effective than a 'Low' one, because no included head-to-head comparison exists beyond one small pilot trial, formulation is confounded with route, design, sponsor and population (as the authors state), and the article reports no statistical test of either difference; whether any effect lasts beyond four weeks after the last dose (only seven studies contributed after the last dose and none later); adverse effects other than all-cause dropout (not analysed); and the size of the effect free of unblinding and small-study bias, which the authors' own funnel-plot analysis suggests inflates the acute estimates.

sample.recruitment: Database search by two authors of Embase, Medline/PubMed, PsycINFO and CENTRAL from inception to 13 April 2023 in any language, with strategies peer-reviewed by a librarian against the PRESS checklist (full strategies in Appendix pp 5-7, not read), plus reference lists of included studies and trial registries; 687 articles identified and 49 RCTs included (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Results, 1st paragraph). Esketamine trial data were also obtained from the Yale University Open Data Access (YODA) Project, which has an agreement with Janssen Research & Development (Acknowledgements). Two-thirds of the trials (33 of 49) recruited treatment-resistant samples (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As stated: randomized controlled trials of ketamine used primarily as a treatment for participants with a clinical diagnosis of major depressive disorder, any language, no start date (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria). The included set is wider than the criterion: Table 1 lists two trials whose entry criteria required failure of a mood stabiliser (Diazgranados 2010; Zarate 2012) and a third whose reference title names bipolar depression (Grunebaum 2017, ref 38), an adolescent trial using the Children's Depression Rating Scale (Dwyer 2021), and trials selected for suicidal ideation (Sinyor 2018; Domany 2020). The registered protocol had specified unipolar or bipolar depression at any age, while its condition field says adults (PROSPERO record, Population; Condition or domain).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article: Table 1 gives design, diagnostic entry criteria, arm sizes, route, formulation, doses and control for each trial, but no age, sex, setting or country, although age, sex and treatment resistance were extracted (Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. For the after-last-dose window the authors report dropouts of 0.0% to 35.5% in the contributing studies and note that this could bias the estimate in either direction (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: The ten esketamine trials include most of the large industry-run trials (seven with 72 to 233 participants in their esketamine arm or arms, Table 1), several of them adding intranasal esketamine or placebo spray to an oral antidepressant (titles of refs 16, 17, 50 and 62), whereas the racemic trials are mostly small single-site intravenous trials, two of them with more than 72 participants in the ketamine arm or arms (Fava 2018; KADS). Three trials enter only through registry results and one through the authors' own then-unpublished trial; data on Janssen trials came partly through YODA. These differences travel with the formulation contrast the review emphasises.

exposure.measurement: Ketamine as given in each trial, classified by the review by formulation, route, number of treatments and dose; doses were converted to an intravenous racemic equivalent using a published review of formulation and route (ref 23) to place each arm in the 'High' or 'Low' category (Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph; Appendix pp 7-8, not read). The authors note that this classification rests on estimates of the parent drug's bioavailability (Discussion, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as listed in Table 1: single doses or courses of 2 to 9 treatments (one oral trial listed with 84 treatments; see reporting issues); intravenous racemic ketamine from 0.1 to 1.0 mg/kg, intravenous esketamine 0.2 and 0.4 mg/kg, intranasal racemic ketamine 50 or 100 mg, intranasal esketamine 28 to 84 mg, subcutaneous racemic ketamine 0.1 to 0.9 mg/kg, intramuscular racemic ketamine, and oral racemic ketamine 50 mg/day or 1.0 mg/kg. The 'High'/'Low' boundary (0.5 mg/kg intravenous racemic equivalent; 84 mg intranasal) is the review's classification of these trial conditions, reported here only as such.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Concomitant medication is not tabulated. Several of the large esketamine trials were add-on designs in which both arms took an oral antidepressant, newly started in two of them (titles of refs 16, 17, 50 and 62; Dean et al., 2021, describe the same design for these trials), which Table 1 does not show; the control in those trials is placebo spray plus an antidepressant, not placebo alone.

comparison.controls: The trials' control arms: saline placebo (27 trials), saline placebo with a bittering agent (5 intranasal esketamine trials), midazolam (14 trials), remifentanil (1), diphenhydramine (1) and an unspecified intranasal spray (1) (Table 1; editors' count). Control type (active or saline) was examined as an effect modifier only in the appendix (pp 49-58, not read).

outcomes.instruments: Depression severity on standardised clinician-rated scales (the review names the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), pooled as SMD of ketamine relative to control (negative favours ketamine); response, defined as a reduction of 50% or more in depressive symptoms; remission, whose definition is not given in the article; acceptability as all-cause dropout at each trial's primary endpoint, only for trials with repeated dosing (Methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard depression scales. The registered protocol defined remission as a HAM-D-17 score of 7 or 8 or less or a MADRS score of 10 or 11 or less (PROSPERO record, Main outcomes); the article does not say which definition was applied.
outcomes.operationalization: Three windows (Methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph): acute, from 4 hours after the first dose to 3 days or the second treatment, whichever came first; repeated dosing, from day 4 to the last treatment (trials with 2 or more sessions); after the last treatment of a course, up to 28 days. Every reported time point inside a window entered the model, with time as linear and quadratic terms, so each window's estimate is an average over time points rather than a value on a fixed day. All effects are measured after dosing, in patients with depression; the review contains no healthy-volunteer data.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p < 0.05 for each estimate. The 10 counts outcome-by-window models (severity, response and remission in three windows, and dropout); together they report about 35 formulation-by-dose estimates plus the time terms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening, risk-of-bias assessment and extraction were done by two authors (SN, AS) with consensus; the Summary says they worked independently, the Methods says they screened 'successively' (Summary › Methods; Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Contributors).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mixed-effects meta-regression estimates with 95% CIs and I-squared; no tau-squared or prediction intervals; no absolute rates. Depression severity (SMD): acute: Rac-High -0.73 (-0.91 to -0.56), Esket-Low -0.55 (-0.87 to -0.24), Esket-High -0.48 (-0.75 to -0.20), Rac-Low -0.33 (-0.54 to -0.12), k = 43, I2 = 60.5%, significant quadratic time term (peak about one day after the dose, then return towards baseline); repeated dosing: Rac-High -0.61 (-1.02 to -0.20), Rac-Low -0.55 (-1.09 to -0.00), Esket-Low -0.15 (-0.49 to 0.19), Esket-High -0.22 (-0.54 to 0.10), k = 16, I2 = 84.2%; after the last dose: racemic -0.65 (-1.23 to -0.07), esketamine -0.33 (-0.96 to 0.31), k = 7, I2 = 87.6%; without the single low-dose arm, racemic -0.87 (-1.43 to -0.31), esketamine -0.32 (-0.81 to 0.16). Response (OR): acute Rac-High 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22), Esket-Low 3.48 (1.66 to 7.27), Rac-Low 2.69 (1.56 to 4.64), Esket-High 2.27 (1.24 to 4.14), k = 37, I2 = 44.0%; repeated Rac-High 2.83 (1.68 to 4.76), Esket-High 1.42 (1.07 to 1.90), Rac-Low 1.56 (0.57 to 4.26), Esket-Low 1.37 (0.91 to 2.05), k = 16, I2 = 37.8%; after the last dose racemic 2.53 (1.00 to 6.37), esketamine 1.76 (0.89 to 3.49), k = 7, I2 = 61.6%. Remission (OR): acute Esket-Low 5.05 (2.41 to 10.54), Rac-Low 3.31 (1.57 to 7.01), Rac-High 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), Esket-High 2.17 (1.43 to 3.29), k = 25, I2 = 9.9%; repeated Rac-High 2.44 (1.49 to 3.99), Esket-High 1.52 (1.27 to 1.82), Rac-Low 1.05 (0.35 to 3.12), Esket-Low 1.30 (0.91 to 1.85), k = 16, I2 = 5.7%; after the last dose esketamine 1.80 (1.14 to 2.82), racemic 1.31 (0.52 to 3.28), k = 7, I2 = 37.7%. All-cause dropout (repeated-dose trials): OR 1.18 (0.85 to 1.64), k = 20, I2 = 17.3%; Rac-Low 0.94 (0.06 to 15.83), Rac-High 1.23 (0.47 to 3.22), Esket-Low 1.06 (0.48 to 2.34), Esket-High 1.20 (0.83 to 1.74).
analysis.covariates: Formulation, dose category and their interaction, with linear and quadratic time, in one model per outcome and window; dose was dropped from the after-last-dose models because only one arm there was low-dose. Other modifiers (control type, treatment resistance, route) were added one at a time to a base model with time only, and their results are only in the appendix (pp 49-58, not read). The authors state that formulation was often confounded with route and that the large parameter space prevented a model with all modifiers (Discussion, 6th paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021221157, first submitted 16 November 2020, version 1.0 published 14 January 2021 (read in this reader's tab; the record still shows the review as planned or ongoing). Differences between the record and the article, none of them mentioned in the article: planned search of MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO in English only, done as five databases in any language; planned risk-of-bias tool RoB 2, used the 2011 Cochrane tool; planned outcomes of suicidality and adverse events (VAS-high, BPRS, CADSS, YMRS, serious adverse events) not reported; planned time points (2-4 hours, 24 hours, day 3-4 and 1 week after a single dose; up to 4 weeks after the first of repeated doses) replaced by three windows including one after the last dose; planned random-effects models and subgroups (titration, route, enantiomer, control type, treatment resistance) replaced by a multivariable meta-regression on a high/low dose category that the record does not mention; planned sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk-of-bias studies not reported; funding given in the record as NHMRC APP1105089 but as none in the article; review team in the record Nikolin and Schwaab with collaborators Loo, Rodgers and Alonzo, while the article adds Bahji, Zarate and Vazquez.
analysis.selective_reporting: The article reports only the formulation-by-dose model; the effect-modifier analyses, per-study risk-of-bias judgments, funnel plots and trim-and-fill estimates are only in the appendix. GRADE is named as the method for rating the body of evidence (Methods › Data analysis, 6th paragraph) but no certainty rating appears anywhere in the article. Suicidality and adverse-event outcomes planned in the protocol are absent without comment. None of the key findings on this card depends on the appendix, except that the risk-of-bias summary and the trim-and-fill result are reported in the article only in outline, with their details in the appendix.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. The after-last-dose window rests on seven studies (four racemic, three esketamine, Discussion 4th paragraph) with one low-dose arm, so dose could not be modelled there. The authors say the acute Esket-Low point estimates are exaggerated by small, underpowered trials (Results › initial effects).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In randomized trials of people with depression, mostly treatment-resistant, ketamine was associated with lower depression scores and higher response and remission than control conditions in the first three days after a first dose for every formulation and dose category (SMD -0.33 to -0.73), with a peak about a day after dosing and a return towards baseline. During repeated dosing, differences in depression scores were significant for racemic ketamine (-0.61 and -0.55) but not for esketamine (-0.15 and -0.22), while response and remission were significant for both 'High' categories and neither 'Low' one. After the last dose (seven studies, up to four weeks) racemic ketamine kept a significant difference in scores and response, esketamine only in remission. All-cause dropout did not differ (OR 1.18). Differences between formulations and doses are comparisons of separate cell estimates from mostly different trials, with no reported test of the difference; heterogeneity was high in the severity models (I2 60.5% to 87.6%); and the funnel-plot analysis suggested missing null results in the acute window.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that higher doses were more effective than low doses and that differences were evident in initial, ongoing and lasting effects after the final dose, and the 'Research in context' panel says higher doses improved outcomes at all stages, including lasting effects. The results contradict this for the after-last-dose window, where dose could not be modelled, and for esketamine in the acute window, where the low-dose estimates exceeded the high-dose ones in all three outcomes; no test of the dose effect is reported in the article. The Discussion opens by calling racemic ketamine superior to esketamine in onset and ongoing treatment, but its next paragraph says the statistical comparison did not differentiate them, and the comparison is confounded with route, trial size, sponsor and add-on design (the authors list several of these confounders as limitations). The abstract calls all acute effects moderate-high, including an SMD of -0.33 that the Results call modest. The conclusion that all doses and formulations were acceptable rests on all-cause dropout alone, which the authors themselves call a coarse measure of safety, and an interval as wide as 0.06 to 15.83 for one cell. The implication for practice, that clinics should adopt protocols ensuring adequate dosing, is drawn from these indirect and confounded comparisons. The Discussion's paragraph on lasting effects misstates which formulation kept a significant effect on depression scores and calls the effects small.

timeline.event: Xu et al., meta-analysis of low-dose and very-low-dose ketamine (9 RCTs, 201 participants, as described in this review's introduction; ref 1); the PROSPERO record calls the present review an update of it by the same group.
Correia-Melo et al., pilot non-inferiority RCT of esketamine against racemic ketamine (ref 66), the only head-to-head trial the authors cite.
Bahji, Vazquez and Zarate, meta-analysis comparing racemic ketamine and esketamine (ref 3; three of its authors are authors of this review).

Dean et al., Cochrane review of ketamine and other glutamate receptor modulators in unipolar depression (searched to July 2020), read in this batch as sc_dean_2021; it overlaps heavily with this review's trials.
Loo et al., KADS trial of repeated subcutaneous racemic ketamine (ref 9), the authors' own trial and the only low-dose arm in the after-last-dose window.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent pooled analysis in this batch and the only one that models time windows and a dose category together. Its pooled acute effects agree in direction with the Cochrane review of Dean et al. (2021), which shares most of its trials, so the two are not independent confirmations. Its formulation and dose conclusions rest on indirect comparisons of different trials and have not been tested in an adequately sized head-to-head randomized trial.

funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of New South Wales and Black Dog Institute, The George Institute for Global Health, Maastricht University, the University of Calgary and the intramural programme of the US National Institute of Mental Health. Review authors are authors of included trials: the KADS trial, called 'our recent phase 3 RCT' (Research in context), and Loo 2016 (Loo first author); Zarate is first author of two included trials (Zarate 2006 and Zarate 2012, refs 13 and 28); Bahji, Vazquez and Zarate wrote the earlier racemic-versus-esketamine meta-analysis (ref 3). No procedure for appraising their own trials is described. CL advises Janssen, the esketamine manufacturer, and CZ holds ketamine-use patents. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An adequately powered randomized head-to-head trial of racemic ketamine against esketamine, each at two doses, on the same route and schedule, with an active control, measured blinding and expectancy, several weeks of repeated dosing and at least three months of follow-up after the last dose, with adverse events (dissociation, blood pressure, bladder, cognition) recorded systematically; and, for the existing trials, an individual-participant meta-analysis that separates formulation from route, trial design, sponsor and population.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (major depressive disorder), intervention (racemic ketamine or esketamine), control conditions and outcomes (severity, response, remission, dropout) are stated; the included set is wider than the stated population (bipolar, adolescent and suicidal-ideation trials), which is recorded as a reporting issue rather than here.

PROSPERO CRD42021221157 was submitted before the review's start date and gives the question, search, eligibility, risk-of-bias tool and a synthesis plan. The article neither mentions nor justifies substantial deviations from it (risk-of-bias tool, search languages, dropped suicidality and adverse-event outcomes, new time windows, a dose classification and meta-regression not in the record, missing risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis, funding).
Randomized trials only, without a stated reason; the choice is conventional for an efficacy question but is not explained.

Five databases, no language or date limit, peer-reviewed strategies (appendix), reference lists and trial registries searched, registry-only results and an unpublished trial included, search about three months before acceptance. Consultation of content experts is not described, which is the one element of the full criterion that is missing.
Two authors with disagreements resolved by consensus; the Summary says independently, the Methods says successively.
Two authors extracted (SN, AS) and three verified (SN, AS, CL) (Summary; Contributors).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article gives no list of excluded full texts; the PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1) is an image and the 9.7 MB appendix, which may hold such a list, was not read (it is a PDF).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives each trial's design, diagnostic entry criteria, arm sizes, formulation, route, doses, number of treatments and control; it gives no age, sex, setting, country, background medication or follow-up times, and not the outcome scale used for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The 2011 Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting), assessed by two authors; per-study judgments are only in the appendix, which was not read, and the article summarises them in one sentence (most studies low or unclear risk).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the article; whether the appendix reports them could not be checked.

A multilevel model with study as random effect and restricted maximum likelihood handles several time points per study; crossover trials enter with first-period data only. Weaknesses not scored by this item: cell estimates are compared without a reported test of the difference, the I-squared of a multilevel model is not explained, and no prediction intervals are given.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias is reported; the protocol's sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk studies does not appear, and the control-type moderator (relevant to blinding) is only in the appendix.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Met narrowly: the limitations discuss compromised blinding in crossover trials and suggest that better-blinded controls in larger trials may explain smaller effects (Discussion, 6th paragraph), but the conclusions on formulation and dose do not carry this through.
I-squared reported for every model (5.7% to 87.6%); effect modifiers examined (results in the appendix) and the confounded parameter space of the trials discussed.

Egger test, contour-enhanced funnel plots and trim-and-fill; the authors report likely missing null results in the acute window and discuss the likely direction (inflated acute effects) and an alternative explanation.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (none) and each author's interests are declared; the record's NHMRC funding and the authors' own included trials are not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 (a critical item) can be judged only from the appendix, which was not read; if it lacks a list of excluded studies with reasons, confidence falls to low. On the items that could be judged, no critical item fails outright (items 2 and 4 are met in part, items 9, 11, 13 and 15 are met), and there are several non-critical weaknesses (items 3 and 12 not met, item 8 met in part, item 10 unknown), which under AMSTAR 2 gives moderate confidence. The rating concerns the pooling, not the conclusions: the review is registered, searched widely, worked in duplicate and examined publication bias, but it departed from its protocol without saying so, and its headline conclusions on formulation and dose go beyond its own estimates. Cite it for the pooled differences by time window and for the scarcity of data after the last dose; do not cite it for racemic ketamine being more effective than esketamine, for a dose-response relationship, or for safety.

key_findings.finding: The search found 687 articles; 49 RCTs with 3299 participants were included (52 control arms, 72 ketamine arms): 45 peer-reviewed trials, 3 trials known from registry results (NCT02106325, NCT03434041, NCT03539887) and one recently completed trial (the authors' KADS trial). 13 trials (27%) were crossovers, for which pre-crossover data were used; 27 (55%) gave a single dose and 22 (45%) repeated doses; 39 (80%) used racemic ketamine and 10 (20%) esketamine; 33 (67%) recruited treatment-resistant samples; ketamine arms were intravenous in 48, intranasal in 17, subcutaneous in 4, oral in 2 and intramuscular in 1.

Risk of bias (2011 Cochrane tool) was low or unclear for most studies (details in Appendix pp 27-28, not read). Contour-enhanced funnel plots showed possible publication bias, and trim-and-fill suggested missing null findings at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, that is, possible bias towards larger acute effects favouring ketamine.

Acute window (4 hours to 3 days after the first or single dose), depression severity: SMD Rac-High -0.73 (95% CI -0.91 to -0.56; p < 0.0001), Esket-Low -0.55 (-0.87 to -0.24; p = 0.0006), Esket-High -0.48 (-0.75 to -0.20; p = 0.0007), Rac-Low -0.33 (-0.54 to -0.12; p = 0.0019); k = 43, I2 = 60.5%. The quadratic time term was significant (0.81, 0.10 to 1.52; p = 0.025), which the authors read as a rapid fall in depression scores peaking about one day after treatment and then returning towards baseline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcome—change in depression severity: initial effects after a single/first dose; Fig. 2 legend
key_findings.note: The authors add that the Esket-Low point estimates from simple meta-analyses at each time point are exaggerated by small, underpowered trials and exceed the model's confidence limits at 4 hours; the model borrows strength from trials that tested both esketamine dose levels.

key_findings.finding: Repeated-dosing window (day 4 to the last treatment), depression severity: racemic ketamine differed from control (Rac-High SMD -0.61, -1.02 to -0.20, p = 0.0038; Rac-Low -0.55, -1.09 to -0.00, p = 0.049); esketamine did not (Esket-Low -0.15, -0.49 to 0.19, p = 0.40; Esket-High -0.22, -0.54 to 0.10, p = 0.18); k = 16, I2 = 84.2%; no significant linear or quadratic time trend.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in depression severity: effects of repeated doses

key_findings.finding: After the last dose of a course (up to 4 weeks): data from 7 studies and 8 ketamine arms, only one of them low-dose (fixed-dose subcutaneous racemic ketamine, the KADS trial), so dose was not modelled. Racemic SMD -0.65 (-1.23 to -0.07; p = 0.029); esketamine -0.33 (-0.96 to 0.31; p = 0.31); k = 7, I2 = 87.6%; trend-level decline over time (p = 0.051). Excluding the low-dose arm: racemic -0.87 (-1.43 to -0.31; p = 0.0023), esketamine -0.32 (-0.81 to 0.16; p = 0.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in depression severity: effects following the final dose of a course of treatments

key_findings.finding: Response (50% or greater reduction in symptoms), acute window: OR Rac-High 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22), Esket-Low 3.48 (1.66 to 7.27), Rac-Low 2.69 (1.56 to 4.64), Esket-High 2.27 (1.24 to 4.14); k = 37, I2 = 44.0%; no significant time terms.

Response during repeated dosing: Rac-High OR 2.83 (1.68 to 4.76) and Esket-High 1.42 (1.07 to 1.90) differed from control; Rac-Low 1.56 (0.57 to 4.26) and Esket-Low 1.37 (0.91 to 2.05) did not; k = 16, I2 = 37.8%. After the last dose: racemic 2.53 (1.00 to 6.37; p = 0.049), esketamine 1.76 (0.89 to 3.49; p = 0.10); k = 7, I2 = 61.6%.

Remission (definition not stated in the article): acute window OR Esket-Low 5.05 (2.41 to 10.54), Rac-Low 3.31 (1.57 to 7.01), Rac-High 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), Esket-High 2.17 (1.43 to 3.29), k = 25, I2 = 9.9%; repeated dosing Rac-High 2.44 (1.49 to 3.99) and Esket-High 1.52 (1.27 to 1.82) significant, Rac-Low 1.05 (0.35 to 3.12) and Esket-Low 1.30 (0.91 to 1.85) not, k = 16, I2 = 5.7%; after the last dose esketamine 1.80 (1.14 to 2.82; p = 0.011), racemic 1.31 (0.52 to 3.28; p = 0.56), k = 7, I2 = 37.7%.

Acceptability, measured only as all-cause dropout at the primary endpoint of trials with repeated dosing, did not differ between ketamine and control: OR 1.18 (0.85 to 1.64; p = 0.31), k = 20, I2 = 17.3%; Rac-Low 0.94 (0.06 to 15.83), Rac-High 1.23 (0.47 to 3.22), Esket-Low 1.06 (0.48 to 2.34), Esket-High 1.20 (0.83 to 1.74). Adverse events were not meta-analysed; the authors call dropout a coarse measure of safety and note that adverse events are dose-dependent in the literature they reviewed.

Definitions used throughout: primary outcome the change in depression severity relative to control on a standardised scale (SMD); response a reduction of at least 50%; three windows (acute from 4 hours after the first dose to day 3 or the second treatment; repeated from day 4 to the last treatment; after the last treatment up to 28 days); acceptability as all-cause dropout in repeated-dose trials. Dose was converted to an intravenous racemic equivalent and classed as 'High' at 0.5 mg/kg or more (or titration up to it), intranasal arms as 'High' when dosing was predominantly at 84 mg or more; this is the review's classification of trial conditions.

Only one small pilot RCT had compared esketamine directly with racemic ketamine (non-inferiority after a single session, ref 66). The authors write that the active-control differences were larger for high-dose racemic ketamine than for esketamine but that the statistical comparison did not significantly differentiate them, and call for large head-to-head RCTs.

Limitations stated by the authors: possible publication or small-study bias (which they suggest may instead reflect a shift from small saline-controlled pilot trials to large trials with better-blinded controls in treatment-resistant samples); dose categories based on estimated bioavailability of the parent drug; compromised blinding and carry-over in crossover trials (handled by using first-period data); many trial features confounded with one another, for example formulation with route, which precluded a comprehensive multivariable model.

Registered protocol (PROSPERO CRD42021221157, version 1.0, 14 January 2021): planned MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO searches restricted to English; population unipolar or bipolar depression of any age; outcomes of depression severity at fixed time points, suicidality, remission (HAM-D-17 of 7 or 8 or less; MADRS of 10 or 11 or less), response, and safety and tolerability (adverse events, dropouts, VAS-high, BPRS, CADSS, YMRS); risk of bias with RoB 2; random-effects models with a sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk studies; funding NHMRC APP1105089; conflicts of interest none known.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'Research in context' panel says higher doses improved outcomes at all stages of a treatment course, including lasting effects, and the abstract says dose differences were evident in lasting effects after the final dose; the Results say dose could not be included in the after-last-dose models because only one arm was low-dose, and the Discussion says data were insufficient to explore dose effects in that period.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Summary › Interpretation; Research in context › Added value of this study; Results › effects following the final dose; Discussion, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim may say this review found a dose effect on lasting benefit.

reporting_issues.issue: The dose conclusion (higher doses more effective) is contradicted for esketamine in the acute window, where the low-dose estimates exceed the high-dose ones for all three outcomes (SMD -0.55 against -0.48; response OR 3.48 against 2.27; remission 5.05 against 2.17), and for acute racemic remission (Low 3.31 against High 2.97). The article reports no test of the dose term; the effect-modifier analyses are in the appendix.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Summary › Interpretation; Results › initial effects; Response rates, 1st paragraph; Remission rates, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose finding is at most a pattern in some cells during repeated dosing (response and remission significant for 'High', not 'Low'), not a demonstrated dose-response relationship.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion paragraph on lasting effects says the follow-up data showed a significant benefit of esketamine and a similar benefit of racemic ketamine once the low-dose arm was excluded, and calls both effects small; in the Results, for depression severity after the last dose racemic ketamine was significant with or without the low-dose arm (SMD -0.65 and -0.87) and esketamine was not (-0.33, p = 0.31; -0.32, p = 0.19); only remission favoured esketamine (OR 1.80) and not racemic ketamine (1.31).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 4th paragraph; Results › effects following the final dose; Remission rates, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The text and the estimates disagree on which formulation kept an effect after the last dose; claims must use the numbers from the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the acute standardised mean differences moderate-high for all conditions, but one of them is -0.33 (Rac-Low), which the Results call modest; the abstract's interpretation says response and remission were numerically greater for racemic ketamine than esketamine, whereas the largest acute remission estimate is Esket-Low (OR 5.05) and after the last dose only esketamine reached significance for remission.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Summary › Findings; Summary › Interpretation; Results)
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's summary of formulation differences holds for depression scores, not for remission.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's first paragraph says racemic ketamine is superior to esketamine in acute onset and ongoing benefit; its second paragraph says the statistical comparison did not significantly differentiate high-dose racemic ketamine from esketamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Superiority is not shown by the review's own analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated inclusion criterion is a clinical diagnosis of major depressive disorder, but Table 1 includes trials requiring failure of a mood stabiliser (Diazgranados 2010; Zarate 2012), a trial whose title names bipolar depression (Grunebaum 2017, ref 38; refs 14 and 28 also name bipolar depression), an adolescent trial (Dwyer 2021) and trials defined by suicidal ideation (Sinyor 2018; Domany 2020); the registered protocol allowed bipolar depression of any age.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Table 1; references 14, 28, 38); registry record (PROSPERO, Population)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimates describe a mixed population (unipolar and bipolar depression, adults and adolescents), not major depressive disorder alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample sizes in Table 1 sum to 3279 when crossover participants are counted once and the 20 lanicemine participants of Downey 2016 (not analysed, footnote b) are left out; the reported total of 3299 equals the sum only if those 20 are included (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 and footnote b)
reporting_issues.consequence: The participant total probably includes 20 people who received a different drug; the analysable total is about 3279.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists the authors' KADS trial as 'Loo et al. (under review)', while reference 9 cites it as published in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 2023.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1, last racemic row; reference 9)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the trial is the published KADS study.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives Arabzadeh 2018 as 84 treatments twice weekly with oral racemic ketamine 50 mg/day and a saline placebo; Dean et al. (2021) describe the same trial as 25 mg twice daily for 6 weeks alongside sertraline, and 84 doses equal 6 weeks of twice-daily dosing (editors' arithmetic), so 'weekly' appears to be an error for 'daily' and the oral comparator cannot have been a saline infusion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1, Arabzadeh et al. (2018) row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the pooled estimates; the row should not be cited for the trial's schedule.

reporting_issues.issue: GRADE is named as the method for rating the quality of the body of evidence, but no GRADE certainty rating is reported anywhere in the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claim writers must rate certainty themselves; the review offers none.

reporting_issues.issue: The article states that there was no funding source; the PROSPERO record gives the National Health and Medical Research Council, Australia (APP1105089), as the funding source. The article also does not mention any of the deviations from the registered protocol (see preregistration detail).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Summary › Funding; Role of the funding source); registry record (PROSPERO, Funding source)
reporting_issues.consequence: A transparency flag; it does not change the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'Research in context' panel says earlier meta-analyses did not examine single versus repeated dosing or route of administration, while the Introduction credits earlier meta-analyses with information on sustained benefit after repeated sessions (ref 2) and on routes of administration (ref 8).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Research in context › Evidence before this study; Introduction, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the novelty claim is overstated.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 describes the comparator of the intranasal esketamine trials only as saline placebo with a bittering agent; the titles of refs 17 and 50 (and Dean et al., 2021, for the same trials) show that these were add-on trials in which both arms started a new oral antidepressant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The esketamine-control differences are differences on top of a newly started antidepressant, which is one reason why they are not comparable with the racemic-control differences from mostly placebo-only trials.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the intravenous esketamine trial of 0.2 and 0.4 mg/kg 'Singh et al. (2016a)' and the twice- or thrice-weekly intravenous racemic ketamine trial 'Singh et al. (2016b)'; Dean et al. (2021) use the opposite labels for the same two trials (Singh 2016 a racemic, Singh 2016 b esketamine). The two reviews also describe the racemic trial's regimen differently: 4 twice-weekly or 6 thrice-weekly treatments here, infusions on days 1 to 25 or 26 (8 or 12 infusions) in Dean et al.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1, Singh et al. rows; references 36 and 37)
reporting_issues.consequence: Risk of mis-citation when the two reviews are compared; identify these trials by journal (Am J Psychiatry 2016 for racemic ketamine, Biol Psychiatry 2016 for esketamine), not by letter.
